ELI5: How do RSS feeds work?

RSS stands for "Really Simple Syndication" and is useful for sites which regularly publish content in discreet 'articles', like Voat.

RSS feeds are loaded by specialized web browsers referred to as Feed Readers, which can run on computers, mobile phones or online (DIGG reader for e.g.: https://reader.digg.com).

Typical RSS users collect feeds from various sources across the web and use their Feed Reader to provide a steady stream of articles from multiple sources. Voat provides RSS feeds for each sub, ELI5 for e.g.: https://voat.co/rss/ELI5

RSS feeds are just a simple file with a computer formatted list of content. They work because an RSS reader refreshes the list at a certain interval (maybe every 5 minutes) so that you can stay up to date with the latest content from that list. It's nothing more than a plain text file updated by a person or a computer program.

rss feeds are like a simple text file that is updated when the owner of the rss feed adds new stuff to his website or podcast. People like you can add these rss "text file" links to a "reader" the so they can keep up to date on the people they're interested in. An rss reader can be a podcast client for on demand radio or even just text articles. Hope this helps. Even craigslist has an rss button so if you want to find out when "free couch" is listed, you click the rss button (after searching with your criteria), copy the url bar contents, add it to your reader so when you're pooping in the morning you have your news and free couch listings in your zip code right there!

You're really potentially asking three different questions:

  • How they work for you as a user:
    Suppose you have a bookmarks bar in your browser. To see whether your favourite bookmarked site has updated, has published a new article/blog post/whatever, you traditionally had to click the bookmark link and load the whole site before you got to see whether there even was anything new or not. Then lather, rinse, repeat. That's inconvenient, and for those on pretty limited bandwidth, it could waste bandwidth and be time-consuming. The RSS system is a technical mechanism that allows any RSS-compatible client (commonly built into your browser, though stand-alone RSS readers did/do still exist) to just load a tiny file containing little more than a notification, hey this is the (new) content I've currently got. Example: Firefox has a built-in RSS reader (that they call Live Bookmarks). Say I want to follow Stephen Baxter's Voynich manuscript posts. I can visit stephenbaxter.net and click on the RSS icon in the top right hand corner and subscribe to the RSS feed via Live Bookmarks and e.g. put that in the Firefox bookmarks bar. Now I can just click on that RSS-bookmark and see that no, there are currently no new articles I haven't read (but there are some older unread ones at the bottom). No reason to click through then – but as soon as there's something new, I'll find it there (provided Mr Baxter updates his feed properly).

  • How they work for you as a web master/site admin:
    There are many scripts that generate RSS feeds automatically, e.g. whenever you post something new on your blog.

  • How they work for you as a developer:
    If you want to write your own implementation, you may have to refer to the specs and tutorials. There are different standards though.

Sadly but perhaps predictably, walled-garden sites like Facebook have reduced/rescinded RSS-compatibility, because RSS is too open, and they really want to control you and ensure that you have to use their systems exclusively.

Btw., there's an RSS button right here in the sidebar. Try it.

It is basically just a list of headlines with a link back to the post/article/whatever. Just add the RSS link to any site/app designed to read RSS feeds, and it'll tell you when that feed updates.

For example, I follow maybe a dozen webcomics. I used to keep up with them using bookmarks, and just check on each of them on their scheduled update day.

When I moved to RSS, I plugged all of their RSS feeds into Feedly, and now I basically have a reddit/voat of webcomics.
